notes.b: Every society has basic needs, such as raising children, passing on knowledge and organising work. A social institution is the lasting, organised way a society meets one of them, which is why institutions matter for understanding family life.
points: A social institution is an established, organised set of norms (accepted rules of behaviour), roles and values built around a basic need of society.
The five main social institutions are the family, education, religion, the economy (work) and government (the State). Health and the media are sometimes added to this list.

An institution is not a building or a single organisation. A school is an organisation within the institution of education, so the school down the road is part of the institution, not the institution itself.

Institutions last across generations, while individual groups come and go. Because they carry norms and values, pass on culture and give structure to social life, each one is an agent of socialisation (a means by which people learn how to behave in society).
Institutions are linked, so what happens in one affects the others. For example, the economy affects family life, and education prepares people for work.
Functionalism is the view that each institution performs functions that help keep society stable. This view describes what institutions do; it does not label any institution good or bad.
A manifest function is an intended and recognised result of an institution, for example the school's function of educating young people.
A latent function is an unintended and often hidden result, for example a school providing supervised care for children while parents are at work.
notes.tip: Do not write that the institution of education is the school. Always tie an institution to a function and an example, because a list of names earns little.

notes.b: The family is the first and most basic institution, because it is where every person's care and learning begins. Over time other institutions take over or add to some of its work.
points: The family reproduces the population and provides for the care of children, older people and dependants (people who rely on others for support).
The family socialises children, passing on language, norms, values and skills, so that children learn how to take part in society.
The family is the basic economic unit of consumption (using goods and services) and provides economic support through shared income and household work.
The family provides emotional security and a sense of belonging and identity.

Other institutions adopt or supplement family functions. Schools take on much of children's education, the State provides welfare and health services, employers provide income, and religious bodies provide moral guidance.

Examples of supplementing a family function: parenting courses support the emotional function, schooling from preschool to third level supports the educational function, welfare payments support the economic function, and medical services support the physical function.
notes.tip: Examiners ask you to explain how one family function has been supplemented by another institution. Name the function (emotional, educational, economic or physical), name the institution, and give one clear sentence linking them.

notes.b: Education is how a society deliberately passes on what it knows, and it also shapes children's behaviour and future work. It works both in the classroom and in the everyday life of the school.
points: Education transmits knowledge, skills and the culture of a society from one generation to the next. It does this formally through the curriculum (the subjects taught), from primary to third level.
It also teaches informally through the hidden curriculum, the unwritten lessons of school life such as rules, punctuality, respect for authority, sharing and teamwork.

Education socialises children, reinforcing the behaviour and values learned at home. It promotes social cohesion by teaching shared history, language and civic values, such as the Irish language and Irish history in Irish schools.

Education prepares people for work through literacy and numeracy, qualifications, specialist skills and career guidance. Work experience comes through Transition Year, the Leaving Certificate Applied, the Leaving Certificate Vocational Programme and college.

Education sorts and allocates people to positions in the economy by means of qualifications. It can support social mobility (moving to a higher social position) by opening access to skilled and professional occupations.

In Ireland, education runs through primary, post-primary, further and higher education. The Leaving Certificate is the state examination at the end of second level, and most students use it for entry to third-level courses.
notes.tip: For a question on the role of education, cover both socialisation (formal teaching, then the hidden curriculum) and preparation for work. For young children, point to social skills learned at home being reinforced through rules, punctuality, respect for authority and teamwork.

notes.b: Education is meant to give everyone a fair chance, but a family's circumstances can affect how far a child gets. Supports exist to narrow that gap.
points: Socio-economic status (a family's income, occupation and social position) affects chances in education. Higher-status families often have more educational opportunities and go on to third level more often.
Costs of books, uniforms and equipment can exclude low-income families, because they cannot afford what a child needs to take part fully.
Grants, book rental schemes and allowances help families meet these costs.
DEIS (Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools) supports aim to reduce the gap for pupils at risk of being left behind.
notes.tip: When asked how socio-economic status affects equality of opportunity, cover costs, parental support, expectations and early school leaving, then the supports that reduce the gap: grants, rental schemes and DEIS.

notes.b: Religion is the institution that answers questions about meaning and right and wrong, and it gives people a community to belong to. Describe it neutrally: Ireland has many faiths and people of no religion.
points: Religion provides a system of beliefs and values that gives meaning to life and explains events that cannot be explained by science alone.
Religion provides moral codes that guide behaviour and reinforce many of a society's norms and values, for example rules against stealing or killing.
Religious rituals mark key stages of life, such as birth, first communion or confirmation, marriage and death.
Religious institutions provide community networks and social support to their members, so people feel they belong.
Churches and other religious bodies have supported education, health care and charity. In Ireland many primary schools still have a religious patron.
The influence of religion on Irish society has changed, with declining influence of the Church, more civil ceremonies and a more secular society (one not guided by religion).
notes.tip: For short questions on religion in family life, say that it marks life stages and offers moral guidance, with one example of each. Describe the historical role of religious patrons neutrally, without value judgements.

notes.b: The economy is the institution that decides how a society produces and shares what people need. Work is how most families connect to it, which is why economic change reaches family life.
points: The economic institution organises the production, distribution and consumption of goods and services.
Employment is the main way the economy allocates status and income to individuals and families, and income decides a family's standard of living.
Economic institutions include businesses, banks, markets and the systems of trade through which goods move between producers and consumers.
Work is where people take on adult roles and learn workplace norms (the accepted behaviour at work).
Economic institutions shape family life, for example by determining whether one or both parents must work outside the home, and so hours of work and childcare needs.
Economic changes affect family income and roles. Unemployment lowers living standards and strains relationships, while growth of service industries creates jobs.
Families are consumers, buying goods and services with the income that work provides.
notes.tip: When asked about the economy and the family, tie the point to a function and an example: for instance, employers provide income, so a family can meet its economic needs.

notes.b: Government is the institution with the power to make rules for everyone and to provide services that individuals cannot organise alone. Its structure spreads that power so no single body holds all of it.
points: The political institution, the State, maintains order, makes laws, collects taxes and provides public services, including social welfare, health, education, housing and protection of the vulnerable.
Government is typically divided into three branches: the legislature, which makes laws; the executive, which carries them out; and the judiciary (the courts), which interprets and applies them.
This division is called the separation of powers, and it prevents any one branch from holding unchecked authority.
In Ireland the Oireachtas, the national parliament, consists of the President, Dáil Éireann and Seanad Éireann. The Government is the executive, and the courts are the judiciary.
Local authorities provide local services such as housing, planning and libraries.
Citizens take part in government by voting in elections and referendums, electing representatives to the Dáil in general elections.
The State supports the family in each function: welfare payments for the economic function, health services for the physical function, and schooling for the educational function.
Child protection is part of this support. The State's agency for children is Tusla, the Child and Family Agency, which has exercised the Child Care Act 1991 functions since 2014.
notes.tip: For short questions on the State and family life, say the State provides welfare, health services and schooling, and give one example for each.

notes.b: Health services and the media are often added to the five main institutions because they also shape everyday life. Treat them as additions, since the list of institutions is not fixed.
points: The health institution promotes health and provides care and treatment for illness and injury.
In Ireland the Health Service Executive (HSE) provides public health care.
The media, including newspapers, radio, television and online platforms, inform the public and entertain it.
The media also shape public opinion and attitudes and transmit norms and values, which makes them both an institution and an agent of socialisation.
The legal system (courts and law) is part of government, so it needs no separate institution.

keyTerms.definition: An organised set of norms, roles and values that meets a basic need of society.
The view that each institution performs functions that help keep society stable.
An intended and recognised result of an institution.
An unintended and often hidden result of an institution.
The division of government into legislature, executive and judiciary, so that no single branch holds unchecked authority.
The national parliament of Ireland, consisting of the President, Dáil Éireann and Seanad Éireann.
The degree to which members of a society share values and feel bound together.
The household, which pools income and shares consumption and work.

factCards.definition: The family, education, religion, the economy and government.
Reproduction of the population, socialisation of children, and care and economic support of its members.
Transmitting knowledge and skills, passing on the culture and national identity, and sorting people into positions by qualification.
The legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out, and the judiciary interprets and applies them.
The President, Dáil Éireann and Seanad Éireann.
A manifest function is intended and recognised; a latent function is unintended and often hidden.

factCards.term: Example of a latent function of school
factCards.definition: Providing supervised care for children while their parents are at work.

questions.prompt: Name three functions of the family as a social institution, and give one example of each.
questions.model: Reproduction of the population, for example through having and raising children. Socialisation of children, for example teaching them language, norms and values in the home. Care and economic support of members, for example caring for an elderly relative or sharing household income and work.

questions.prompt: Discuss how the education system and the economy contribute to the stability of society, and explain how each can also be a source of change.
questions.model: Education transmits knowledge, skills and culture from one generation to the next, promotes social cohesion through shared language and history, and sorts people into positions in the economy by qualifications. Education can produce change by opening access to skilled occupations and so supporting social mobility. The economy organises production, distribution and consumption, and allocates status and income through employment. Its stability depends on the employment it provides, and it can produce change when the occupational structure shifts, for example through the growth of professional and service jobs, which changes the balance of socio-economic groups and the pattern of family life.
